lesson.title: The -CIÓN Bridge
lesson.subtitle: Hundreds of nouns convert whole: tradición, confirmación — and every one takes la

hook.title: The Most Generous Bridge in Spanish
hook.content: Every English noun ending in -tion converts directly into Spanish -ción. Collection becomes colección. Tradition becomes tradición. Confirmation becomes confirmación. And best of all: you never have to guess grammatical gender. Every single -ción and -sión noun is 100% feminine and takes la.

pattern.title: -CIÓN Guarantees Feminine Gender — and 'La' Means 'It'
pattern.content: Because Latin abstract nouns in -tiō were feminine, every single descendant in Spanish takes la. The acute accent on ó tells your voice to stress the final syllable: tra-di-CIÓN, con-fir-ma-CIÓN. And when you refer back to one of these feminine words as 'it', the walking pronoun is la: La quiero ('I want it').
pattern.linguist_note: Latin -tiōnem evolved to Spanish -ción with palatalization of the dental stop. Stress is always oxytone (aguda).
pattern.trap_note: Learners sometimes wonder if any -ción noun takes el. The answer is zero: every -ción noun in Spanish takes la.

summary.takeaway: -ción guarantees feminine gender for over a thousand nouns without memorization.

foreshadow.line: Every one of these -ción nouns hides an active verb waiting to be released. In Topic 3, we unlock the engine that turns nouns into action.

payoff.text: In Topic 1, la was waiting for its true partner. Here it is: every single -ción noun is feminine and takes la.

colección.etymology_derivation: Latin collectiōnem. The -CIÓN ending is your passport: thousands of words convert, and every one takes la.

tradición.etymology_derivation: Latin trāditiō ('a surrender, handing over') — tradition is knowledge handed across generations.

confirmación.etymology_derivation: Latin confirmātiō. Accent on the ó marks the stressed final syllable.

organización.etymology_derivation: Latin organizātiō. Spanish spells with z where British English uses s.

opinión.etymology_derivation: Latin opīniō. Like -ción, words in -sión and -ión are consistently feminine.

reservación.etymology_derivation: Latin reservātiō. Also heard as la reserva in Spain.

la.etymology_derivation: Latin illa → la. It functions as both the feminine definite article ('the') and the direct object pronoun ('her / it').

querer.etymology_derivation: Latin quaerere ('to seek, ask for') evolved in Spanish to 'to want' and 'to love'. When you make an inquiry in English, you are asking what you want.

lo.etymology_derivation: Latin illum → lo. Walks one step to the left of conjugated verbs: I it want.

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).
